Here's an example PC I came up with: http://pcpartpicker.com/user/TremorAcePV/saved/MKzbt6 That website is glorious for finding and comparing PC parts.

Reasons I chose some of those parts:

  • SSDs make the user experience notably better. Always. I've yet to find a situation where an HDD was worth the trade-off in speed for the space.
  • A Quad core CPU is preferred for multi-tasking. Dual-core is never worth it.
  • 8GB of RAM is good enough for most people at this time. The thing with RAM is you never notice when you have too much but you always notice when you have too little. Never skimp. Ever. It cripples your system when you skimp on RAM. Always get good quality RAM too.
  • Some people are going to go "Mini-ITX... are you sure?" but I have yet to find a reason to go larger except that it's easier to build-in, but that's why I chose the SFX PSU. Some may go "But what if he wants to upgrade?" but I can tell you most 90%+ of people don't bother and if they do, they do so when they get a new PC all-together so ¯\_(ツ)_/¯
  • Don't use a TV. Just don't. There are many reasons why, but first and foremost is what is known as "input lag". Input lag is the time it takes for you doing something with a peripheral (a gamepad/controller or a mouse) to show up on the monitor/TV. TV's tend to have notable input lag. Computer monitors tend to not. The monitor I listed in that part list is a nice one for what it is. Input Lag affects user experience. Meaning you can physically tell when something is updating slower than you are controlling it and this is jarring. This is why I push SSDs. This is why I say never to use TVs (some TVs have ok input lag but it's best to just avoid in general). It's all about best user experience and this is the best way I know to get it.

To clarify some above terms:

  • Mini-ITX - This is a form factor. A form factor is a standardized size in building that has specific dimensions. Mini-ITX is the smallest form factor that is widely used at this time. The "TX" form factors are specifically for the motherboard size. Sizes are thus: Mini-ITX < Micro-ATX < ATX.
  • PC Cases - These are classified by the largest Motherboard they support and pretty much all cases support a motherboard smaller than their largest size. So, a case that supports an ATX motherboard will support Micro-ATX and Mini-ITX as well. PC Cases have different designations based on size though. ATX Desktop is a more generic term for a case that lays on it's side, but ATX Full Tower is larger than ATX Mid Tower and both those are meant to stand up (but don't have to).
  • SFX PSU - Small Form Factor Power Supply Unit. PSU's come in Form Factors as well. Most are ATX and will fit in any ATX-type case (ATX or Micro-ATX). The EPS12V and BTX versions are ignoreable because they support ATX as well. SFX is special though. They usually come with an adapter for larger cases, but SFX PSUs are notably smaller than ATX and this makes them best for using in Mini-ITX cases.

While I'm technically a combo gamer (I usually adopt the consoles several years after they have been released from the secondhand market, and have had their prices dropped significantly), I've always been rather a fan of PC gaming. For multiple reasons:

  • Consoles, you have to buy a new machine every generation. PC's, you just swap some parts out for the newer, better model of said parts, and a single mobo will outlast the machine itself, assuming you take good care of it.

  • Consoles, you are tied to one particular method of release, and you aren't going to play any games the particular consolemaker doesn't want you to play. Square Enix signed an exclusivity deal with Sony, but you want to play the game on your Microsoft console? Too bad, no Final Fantasy for you. Meanwhile, with the advent of emulators, even if you have to wait several years for the emulators to catch up with the consoles, you can still play any title your emulators can play, on a PC.

  • At the end of the day, Consoles are about controlling what the consumer can do and who they buy from, through control of the code and through licensing. You could technically argue that this results in higher-quality games, and on some levels, you would be correct. But it does absolutely nothing to keep the distributor from issuing shovelware titles. I point to the vast clone-library of the NES and the Madden/NHL/MLB series for the PS2, where assets where re-used repeatedly and infamously. In effect, this amounts to a one-sided control mechanism, which puts the consumer entirely at the mercy of the distributor, and dependent upon them to not issue shit-tier games. In short, it's an anti-consumer practice.

In short, I prefer PC Gaming, because the combination of my skills at repairing/upgrading/building PC's combined with my own freedom of code and products makes it the most economic choice for me. I've also found that as more people grow older and become more capable/self-sufficient, they tend to develop a bent towards PC Gaming, at least amongst the tech-savvy. That may help to explain what you're experiencing.

I see you've made your edit to the OP, but I just want to throw you my thoughts, considering I was in a similar position to you just over a year ago now (built my PC in June 2015 if memory serves). I also don't know what country you're in, but chances are it's either UK or US (I'm in the UK, but I know that the US has great deals on PC components compared to UK). I toyed with the idea of building a PC for a couple years or so before I finally pulled the trigger, so having done extensive research before hand, and having gone through it myself, I'd like to think at least a little bit that my opinion has a little weight. On the other hand, I'm a 'random internet stranger', so feel free to pinch of salt this if you so choose.

First thing to note, building a PC is expensive. I won't say I got caught out, but it was more expensive than I thought it would be. The PC I'm typing this out on cost me just a little over £800. The UK has just voted Brexit, so the £ is going up and down like a yoyo, but if I recall correctly, that translated to around $1200 (was doing a lot of comparisons, contemplated shipping parts here at one point, just saying, I explored a lot of avenues for how best to do it). It looks like £800 now is around $1100, I don't know if it was around $1200, sounds a little high, but over $1000 certainly (again, only relevant if you're in the US). But a fairly sizable chunk of cash regardless.

Secondly, and this is related to price. Don't skimp out on parts - building a PC can be expensive for a reason. My ultimate aim was to have a very solid foundation that I can utilize in the future, and not necessarily be cheap. Sure, a Corsair 600W PSU could have done the job, but here I am with my EVGA 750W - not only giving me overhead (and actually meeting the recommendation of my GPU), but a part that is recommended highly as the build quality is very good. Sure, there are the same GPUs under a different brand that are £50-70 cheaper than mine - but here I am with the one that runs the coolest on all the benchmarks (which actually saved my ass once as I was running a game at a temperature that the other GPUs probably would have melted at). Not necessarily for the GPU, but the PSU I can definitely reuse. The i5 processor which more than meets my needs, I can definitely reuse when I upgrade to a much better motherboard than the one I purchased to cut corners. SO I was willing to go a little overboard for the sake of the higher quality, and on some parts, added reusability.

Also, building a PC is not as simple as it seems. Sure, you can burn through 'how to build a PC', but the level of stop-starting I did on this shit and checking stuff made my PC build go over 2 days (did it at the weekend). Not saying it's a misconception, I'm sure PC builders who do it for a living are very skilled and quick at their job, but the average PC gamer - or at least first time builder - I wouldn't be surprised if you don't get it done in an day. (Admittedly, I started it in the afternoon, but I still wouldn't rush it if you're hesitant about how something goes etc).

Another term you'll see is 'future-proofing'. What this is referring to is of course, purchasing parts that are top of the line now so you don't need to be able to have to buy better parts soon after building. As tech is ever advancing, this is simply a myth. The only future-proofing you'll actually have happen is things nobody thinks about, like case fans - a case fan will always have the same job. Sure, there are ones that are better, ones with LEDs, but the purpose will stay the same. They're as future proof a product as you can get.

Now I've rambled for a while here, and it's already reached 2am, so I'm gonna quickly highlight the other side to building - the actual games.

Take a look at Steam. I presume you know what Steam is, but in case you didn't, basically the main place you'll buy all your games. People will say Steam is the worst thing since sliced bread because of the DRM, when in actual fact, it offers some of the best prices you'll ever see, and it's where the majority of your games will come from. The prices here are because of the Summer Sale, but this is admittedly when most PC gamers bulk up on games that they like, some they'll never play, and anything else that involves buying games. Search for the first 20 games you'll buy. I say 20, because unless they're on here, I'd question going PC. What I mean is, PC has a lot of games. Anything on console that's multiplatform, plus all the indie hipster garbage, given that PC is the easiest platform to develop for (or at least publish for). So if you already own a lot of what you're interested in, then you may want to hold off.

Now go to this subreddit on 'that other site' Reddit. Look at the price range people have, and find posts people have made that are similar to yours (or make one yourself if you're a sneaky snake like that). Now go to YouTube, and look up those games you're interested in, plus type in the graphics card that you're most likely going to be getting. See the performance it hits, and what graphics settings it's on to achieve whatever it's getting. Is this performance you're satisfied with? Are the graphics pretty enough? Optimization is another big player, so it's no good going by just what year the graphics card you're buying is from with what year the game released in. Some games are much better than others. MGSV is very well optimized, Arma 3 not so much. See what people are getting. See what you'll potentially be getting.

I'm going to head off, and I can elaborate further on anything I may have mentioned (I'm certainly not re-reading it now), and answer any questions you'd like. I'd definitely continue to let the idea simmer for a while though. See if you're really hankering for a nice PC, or just a bit of a temporary daydream. I don't mean that offensively, but I've known plenty of people to not think things through, and it doesn't work out well.
